caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
data_source: IMF World Economic Outlook via DataMapper (latest vintage, accessed October 2026)
debt_management: Swiss debt has fallen through the period: 47.7% of GDP in 2006 (the series high), 42.4% in 2020, a low of 35.9% in 2022, and a projected 39.4% in 2025. The constitutional debt brake — in force since 2003 — is the anchor, and it has delivered structural surpluses in good years. GDP more than doubled from $448.5bn in 2006 to a projected $1,043.5bn in 2025. Debt sustainability is beyond question; Switzerland borrows at the world's lowest rates and the fiscal debate is about spending the surpluses, not financing deficits.
inflation_management: The Swiss National Bank targets price stability (defined as 0-2%), and Switzerland had the developed world's best inflation record: -0.5% in 2009, -1.1% in 2015 (the low) after the franc-cap removal, -0.7% in 2020 — chronic undershooting, not overshooting. The 2022 shock produced just 2.8%, the series high, barely above the target band, on franc strength and early SNB hiking. It was 1.1% in 2024 and is projected at 0.2% for 2025 — back to the deflationary edge. The franc's safe-haven appreciation is the permanent disinflationary force; the SNB spent the 2010s fighting it with negative rates and intervention.

key_events.event: Financial crisis: UBS was rescued by the state and SNB (2008); the franc surged as a safe haven.
SNB imposed the franc cap vs the euro (2011); its sudden removal (January 2015) caused -1.1% inflation.
Negative-rate era: the SNB held rates at -0.75% for years to fight franc strength.
Energy shock produced only 2.8% inflation, the series high — the developed world's mildest.
Credit Suisse collapse and UBS takeover (March 2023); inflation projected at 0.2% in 2025.

outlook_next_decade: Switzerland's outlook is one of stability with a deflationary bias: the franc's structural strength keeps inflation at or below target, and the debt brake keeps debt falling. The banking-sector concentration after the UBS-Credit Suisse merger is the main domestic risk, now explicitly a too-big-to-fail question for a small economy. Growth is steady but slow; the analytical assessment is that Switzerland's macro risks are external — a euro-area crisis would hit through the franc — not fiscal or monetary.
